chunks.section: Spectral and Subspace Dynamics of LoRA in Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning
chunks.text: Chenruo Liu † † thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: New York University Zihan Wang 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: New York University Yijun Dong Affiliation: Institute of Science and Technology Austria Qi Lei Affiliation: New York University

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is commonly used in both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), often under similar optimizer settings. Yet, how the different dynamics of the two stages manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimizes remains unclear. Tracking the singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates on mathematical reasoning tasks, we find that RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate, while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; moreover, RL rotates the singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. A quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA unveils the underlying mechanism: group-mean baseline subtraction tilts the balance between two competing forces, coherent fitting and gradient noise, toward spectral concentration and faster subspace rotation, while forcing the risk-favorable learning rate to be low. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor LoRA updates to each stage: in SFT, we flatten the spectrum of the full update to spread adaptation across singular directions, whereas in RL, we flatten the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span to promote subspace rotation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks across multiple models show that the respective configurations for SFT and RL yield the best performance among the compared methods in most evaluated settings.

Post-training is an essential step in modern deep learning that adapts a powerful pre-trained model with general knowledge to specialized downstream tasks. A common post-training pipeline consists of two stages: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which first equips the pre-trained model with primary domain knowledge through off-policy expert demonstrations, followed by reinforcement learning (RL), which further improves the model through its own on-policy responses guided by reward signals like human feedback [ 25 , 32 , 27 ] or verifiable correctness checks [ 33 , 44 ] . During post-training, parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 11 ] are commonly incorporated to reduce the memory and compute footprint. Specifically for LoRA, a frozen pretrained weight W 0 W_{0} is adapted by a low-rank update Δ ​ W t = α r ​ B t ​ A t \Delta W_{t}=\frac{\alpha}{r}B_{t}A_{t} , with trainable factors B t ∈ ℝ d o × r B_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{o}\times r} and A t ∈ ℝ r × d i A_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{i}} of rank r ≪ min ⁡ { d o , d i } r\ll\min\{d_{o},d_{i}\} , scaled by α \alpha . In practice, the LoRA factors B t , A t B_{t},A_{t} are often trained by the same optimizer like Adam [ 17 ] under nearly identical settings in both SFT and RL.

However, SFT and RL demonstrate distinct behaviors during post-training, suggesting different dynamics that can be benefited from tailored optimization strategies. For example, compared to SFT, RL tends to generalize better out of distribution [ 5 , 18 ] , forget less [ 4 , 34 ] , and update sparser subnetworks [ 24 ] . RL is also usually run with markedly smaller learning rates compared to SFT [ 37 , 33 ] . While numerous differences between SFT and RL have been observed through model outputs, hidden representations, and full weight matrices, in the context of LoRA, much less is known about how such differences manifest in the low-rank increment Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} that LoRA actually optimizes. Filling this gap is a prerequisite for tailoring LoRA optimization to the distinct dynamics of SFT and RL. We investigate the dynamics of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} through two complementary lenses: the spread of singular values measured by the effective rank [ 30 ] that determine how the knowledge required for the downstream task is distributed over the r r available directions, and the rotation of the left and right singular subspaces that determine which input and output directions are used. We ask through these lenses: How do SFT and RL differ in the spectrum and singular subspaces of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} ; what is the mechanism that drives these differences; and how can LoRA optimization be tailored to each stage?

chunks.section: Baseline subtraction separates the LoRA dynamics of SFT and RL (Section 2 ).
chunks.text: Across various Llama and Qwen models on GSM8K [ 6 ] and MATH [ 9 ] , we observed that RL with verifiable reward via group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [ 33 ] concentrates the spectrum of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} at every learning rate; whereas SFT expands it at moderate learning rates that can facilitate desired downstream performance. For the dynamics of the singular subspaces, we observed that RL with small learning rates rotates the singular subspace much faster than SFT. Moreover, interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we find that both contrasts appear only once a group-mean baseline is subtracted from the reward, pinpointing baseline subtraction as the key mechanism that separates the LoRA dynamics of SFT and RL.

chunks.section: Baseline subtraction tilts the balance between coherent fitting and gradient noise (Section 3 ).
chunks.text: To understand these contrasts, we analyze a quadratic multi-index model in which a LoRA adapter is trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on pairs of correlated inputs, each pair modeling a GRPO group of responses sampled for the same prompt. Two forces compete in this model: coherent fitting that is linear in the learning rate and concentrates spectral energy on strongly responding directions, as well as feedback from gradient noise that is quadratic in the learning rate and redistributes the spectral energy more evenly. Subtracting a group-mean baseline largely cancels the gradient component shared across a group’s responses, which drives coherent fitting along pretrained directions and anchors successive updates to similar directions, while retaining most of the component that contrasts responses within the group, and damping the gradient noise from task-irrelevant directions. Coherent fitting thus persists through the contrasts while the redistributing feedback loses relative strength, and gradient noise, no longer anchored by the shared component, steers the update directions more, leading to spectral concentration and faster singular subspace rotation during RL. Nevertheless, baseline subtraction can come at a cost for prediction: coherent fitting of the shared component reduces the risk more efficiently than fitting of the contrasts, cancellation of which shrinks the risk reduction from coherent fitting (linear in the learning rate) relative to the cost of gradient noise (quadratic in the learning rate). The risk-favorable learning rate thus remains low, consistent with the common practice in RL.

chunks.section: The dynamics inform stage-specific LoRA optimization (Section 4 ).
chunks.text: Our analysis further shows which dynamics accompany the risk-favorable learning rate: training without a baseline (as in SFT) expands the spectrum of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} , whereas training with a baseline (as in RL) concentrates the spectrum and rotates the left singular subspace faster. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor the update of LoRA factors to each stage by combining two standard components, a norm-preserving spectral flattening as in Muon [ 14 ] and a per-factor choice between SGD and Adam update directions. In SFT, we flatten the singular spectrum of the full update of the factor so that the adaptation is distributed more evenly across singular directions; whereas in RL, we flatten only the component of the update orthogonal to the current left singular subspace of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} , which promotes subspace rotation while leaving the within-subspace component unchanged. The resulting configurations achieve dominating downstream performance across most evaluated models and tasks.

chunks.section: Differences between supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning.
chunks.text: Prior work has characterized differences between SFT and RL at the output, representation, and parameter levels. At the output level, empirical studies report stronger out-of-distribution performance under RL than SFT [ 18 , 5 ] . Subsequent work further highlights the dependence of SFT generalization on optimization, data quality, and model capability [ 29 ] . Beyond performance, studies examine the diversity of generated outputs: RLHF reduces overall response diversity relative to SFT [ 18 ] , while analyses distinguishing correct and incorrect reasoning trajectories find that SFT expands the former and RL compresses the latter [ 21 ] . Moreover, a line of work examines how changes in the model’s output distribution during fine-tuning relate to the preservation of pretrained capabilities. These studies illustrate how on-policy RL can better preserve distributional modes associated with prior knowledge than SFT [ 4 ] , and link RL’s better retention to an implicit preference for output distributions closer to that of the initial model in KL divergence [ 34 ] . At the hidden representation level, Shi et al. [35] find that SFT rapidly introduces specialized features that stabilize early, whereas RL induces more restrained but continually evolving feature changes.

chunks.section: Differences between supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning.
chunks.text: At the parameter update level, studies report greater sparsity in parameter updates under RL than SFT [ 24 ] . Comparisons of update vectors across tasks reveal large absolute cosine similarities under SFT, whereas RL updates are nearly orthogonal [ 50 ] . Spectral analyses of the weight matrices further show smaller changes from the pretrained spectra and principal subspaces under RLVR than SFT [ 49 ] . Our work also compares spectral and subspace dynamics under SFT and RL. In contrast, we focus on the LoRA update matrix itself, track how its spectral concentration and subspace rotation vary with learning rate and training step, interpolate between SFT and RL through intermediate training settings to identify where these differences arise, and use these findings to guide the choice of optimizer configurations for LoRA in each paradigm.

chunks.section: Spectral and subspace analyses for LoRA optimization.
chunks.text: Prior work uses spectral and subspace analyses to study LoRA and improve it through subspace selection and the allocation of singular values. From a subspace perspective, PiSSA initializes adapters with principal singular components of pretrained weights and reports faster convergence and better task performance than standard LoRA [ 22 ] . MiLoRA instead initializes adapters with minor singular components to preserve pretrained knowledge, and its analysis shows less forgetting than PiSSA [ 40 ] . Beyond using pretrained weights alone, further work incorporates downstream task information to guide the initialization of LoRA subspaces. LoRA-One initializes LoRA factors to align with the principal singular subspaces of the initial full gradient [ 48 ] . Xu et al. [41] study how LoRA factors align with task-relevant directions in a matrix factorization setting and propose a spectral initialization informed by both pretrained weights and the downstream task. Moving from initialization to training, SDC-LoRA finds that LoRA updates can drift toward pretrained principal singular subspaces even with MiLoRA’s minor-subspace initialization. It further reduces forgetting by downscaling the gradient components aligned with these principal subspaces during training [ 45 ] .

chunks.section: Spectral and subspace analyses for LoRA optimization.
chunks.text: Another line of work examines the allocation of singular values in LoRA update matrices. Kang et al. [15] apply Muon to LoRA and observe more uniform growth of singular values, with effective ranks close to the nominal LoRA rank. Spectral Surgery finds that some singular components of trained LoRA update matrices contribute little to task performance or are even detrimental. It therefore reweights their singular values after training while keeping the learned singular directions fixed to improve task performance [ 36 ] . While the above studies address general LoRA optimization and are primarily evaluated in supervised settings, recent work develops methods specifically for RLVR. GeoRA argues that PiSSA’s emphasis on pretrained principal directions can conflict with RLVR’s need to preserve pretrained structure. It therefore uses spectral and weight-magnitude information to construct a masked weight matrix and initializes LoRA adapters from its principal singular components [ 46 ] . Similarly, Zhang et al. [47] find that PiSSA and MiLoRA can become unstable under RLVR despite their benefits in SFT. They link this instability to singular-value scaling at initialization and propose an orthonormal initialization that avoids this scaling. In contrast, we compare spectral and subspace dynamics under SFT and RL, and use the observed differences to guide the choice of optimizer configurations for LoRA during training in each setting.

Moreover, to characterize subspace rotation between training steps t 1 t_{1} and t 2 t_{2} , we measure the overlaps of their left and right singular subspaces: ovlp L ⁡ ( t 1 , t 2 ) \displaystyle\operatorname{ovlp}_{L}(t_{1},t_{2}) = 1 r ​ ‖ U t 1 ⊤ ​ U t 2 ‖ F 2 ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{r}\left\|U_{t_{1}}^{\top}U_{t_{2}}\right\|_{F}^{2}\in[0,1], ovlp R ⁡ ( t 1 , t 2 ) \displaystyle\operatorname{ovlp}_{R}(t_{1},t_{2}) = 1 r ​ ‖ V t 1 ⊤ ​ V t 2 ‖ F 2 ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{r}\left\|V_{t_{1}}^{\top}V_{t_{2}}\right\|_{F}^{2}\in[0,1], where, over the same training interval, smaller overlap values indicate faster subspace rotation.

Throughout this work, we use GRPO [ 33 ] as a representative RL algorithm. To identify the sources of differences in effective rank and subspace overlap between SFT and RL, we consider a ladder of four training settings that interpolate between the two: (i) SFT, which performs supervised training on gold completions; (ii) Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT), which replaces gold completions with model-generated completions and trains only on correct ones, corresponding to training weights r i r_{i} for binary rewards r i ∈ { 0 , 1 } r_{i}\in\{0,1\} ; (iii) RFT with group-mean baseline subtraction (RFT-B), which introduces baseline subtraction into RFT, changing the weights from r i r_{i} to r i − r ¯ r_{i}-\bar{r} , where r ¯ \bar{r} is the mean reward over all completions for the same prompt; and (iv) GRPO, which extends RFT-B to online sampling and additionally incorporates GRPO optimization mechanisms, including policy ratio clipping and fixed-length loss normalization following Dr. GRPO [ 20 ] , without KL regularization.

Our model suite includes the base and instruction-tuned variants of Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.2-3B [ 7 ] , Qwen2.5-3B [ 26 ] , and Qwen2.5-Math-7B [ 42 ] , yielding eight models in total. We conduct experiments on the mathematical reasoning benchmarks GSM8K [ 6 ] and MATH [ 9 ] , with the MATH results provided in Appendix A.1 . We use LoRA with rank r = 16 r=16 and scaling parameter α = 32 \alpha=32 , applied to all eligible linear modules in the transformer blocks. In Figure 1 and Figures 3 , 5 , and 6 in Appendix A.1 , GRPO consistently exhibits decreasing effective rank as training progresses across all learning rates considered. In contrast, the effective rank dynamics of SFT depend on the learning rate: effective rank decreases at both small and large learning rates, while at intermediate learning rates from 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} to 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} , it begins to increase after approximately 25 training steps. For models that benefit from SFT 1 1 1 Not all models improve under SFT, as observed in our experiments and in prior studies that fine-tune LLMs on GSM8K and MATH [ 28 , 16 ] , consistent with findings that effective SFT depends on the training data and base-model capability [ 43 , 29 ] . , this intermediate regime also yields the best SFT performance (Table 5 in Appendix A.2 ). This observation is consistent with prior findings that both excessively small and large learning rates can impair LoRA SFT performance [ 8 , 3 ] , and further suggests that a less concentrated singular value distribution accompanies more effective adaptation in these settings. Moreover, RFT-B mirrors GRPO in exhibiting decreasing effective rank across all learning rates considered, whereas RFT shares with SFT an intermediate learning rate regime in which effective rank increases. This comparison identifies group-mean baseline subtraction as a key factor underlying the contrasting spectral dynamics.

Figure 2 and Figures 4 , 7 , and 8 in Appendix A.1 compare the subspace overlap dynamics across training settings. First, the dominant rotation depends on the LoRA initialization: under B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 , the decrease in overlap is generally more pronounced for the left singular subspace, whereas under A 0 = 0 A_{0}=0 , it is more pronounced for the right singular subspace. Second, at small learning rates, GRPO exhibits a markedly faster decrease in overlap than SFT (in the left subspace under B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 and in the right subspace under A 0 = 0 A_{0}=0 ), indicating more rapid rotation of the LoRA singular subspaces. As the learning rate increases, this gap narrows. Together with the use of smaller learning rates for RL than for SFT in prior studies [ 37 , 33 ] , this pattern suggests that promoting subspace rotation may benefit RL adaptation. Moreover, as with effective rank, GRPO and RFT-B exhibit similar rotation dynamics, while SFT and RFT form another qualitatively similar pair. These comparisons point to baseline subtraction as the primary source of the observed spectral and subspace differences in our setting, rather than differences in completion sources between SFT and RFT, or online sampling and other implementation details distinguishing RFT-B from GRPO. These findings motivate a theoretical understanding of how baseline subtraction shapes spectral concentration and subspace evolution, how these effects depend on the learning rate, and how they relate to prediction risk.

The comparison between RFT and RFT-B in Section 2 suggests that subtracting a group baseline can change how a LoRA adapter learns. We study this mechanism in a model that connects effective rank, singular-subspace rotation, and the learning rates favorable for prediction.

The effective-rank trend reflects competition between fitting and redistribution across directions. Coherent fitting favors strongly responding directions, concentrating singular-value energy. Gradient noise, the variation of the stochastic gradient across sampled groups, produces feedback that counteracts this concentration. At leading order in the small task perturbation, the Gram-matrix update has cross terms linear in η \eta and gradient-square terms quadratic in η \eta , so the feedback gains relative influence at larger rates. Normalizing the spectral energy removes uniform growth: effective rank increases only when relative energy becomes more evenly distributed. Baseline subtraction acts differently on shared responses and within-group contrasts. Products of shared coordinates have correlation ρ a 2 \rho_{a}^{2} across the pair, whereas products of shared and newly useful coordinates have correlation ρ a ​ ρ o \rho_{a}\rho_{o} . Subtracting the pair mean therefore retains fractions ϑ a = ( 1 − ρ a 2 ) / 2 < 1 / 2 \vartheta_{a}=(1-\rho_{a}^{2})/2<1/2 and ϑ o = ( 1 − ρ a ​ ρ o ) / 2 > 1 / 2 \vartheta_{o}=(1-\rho_{a}\rho_{o})/2>1/2 of their respective residual energies. Similar responses largely cancel, while contrasting responses survive more strongly and continue to drive fitting. When contrasts carry enough task energy, this dispersing feedback loses more relative strength than concentration after spectral normalization. A large learning rate is then needed for redistribution to dominate, allowing to increase effective rank without a baseline and decrease it with one. At the low rate, fitting dominates in both cases.

Rotation measures how much the span of the adapter’s columns changes between checkpoints. Shared responses repeatedly pull updates toward similar directions, helping to stabilize this span across sampled groups. Baseline subtraction suppresses these responses more strongly than within-group contrasts, as reflected by ϑ a < ϑ o \vartheta_{a}<\vartheta_{o} . Differences between sampled groups consequently have greater influence on the directions of subsequent updates. Then the span changes more between records, giving smaller left singular-subspace overlap. For risk, the leading prediction gain is linear in the learning rate, while gradient noise contributes a quadratic cost. In this model, fitting the task component along pretrained directions gives more prediction progress per unit residual energy. Since ϑ a < ϑ o \vartheta_{a}<\vartheta_{o} , baseline subtraction suppresses this shared component more strongly, reducing useful progress relative to the noise cost. The favorable learning-rate range therefore shifts downward, yielding the opposite rate preferences in the theorem.

The theorem predicts effective-rank growth over a suitable range of learning rates, consistent with the intermediate-rate growth for SFT/RFT in Figure 1 (Section 2.2 ). The theoretical high-rate regime has an upper limit, making a different trend at the largest tested rates. The leading-order rotation gap also narrows as the learning rate increases over the proved comparison range. Intuitively, larger rates amplify an additional source of rotation from gradient noise. At fixed adjacent updates, this contribution grows quadratically with the rate and is stronger without a baseline, which retains both the group-average and within-group components. It therefore offsets part of the extra rotation caused by baseline subtraction, consistent with the narrowing empirical separation in Figure 2 . Appendix C.7 gives the coefficient comparison.

The risk comparison first supports different learning-rate choices for SFT and group-relative RL. In the model, the favorable higher rate without a baseline accompanies growing effective rank, whereas the favorable lower rate with a baseline accompanies greater left singular-subspace motion than without a baseline at that same rate. The geometry at these respective rates then motivates different update priorities: distributing adaptation across singular directions for SFT and promoting motion outside the current left singular subspace for RL. Section 4.1 develops these ideas through a spectral transformation of the full update for SFT and of its component orthogonal to the current left singular subspace for RL. The specific optimizer combinations are evaluated in Section 4.2 .

Motivated by the empirical findings in Section 2 and the theoretical analysis in Section 3 , we select dynamics-informed configurations of standard optimizer components for LoRA in SFT and RL, with GRPO as the RL algorithm. Each configuration combines existing ingredients, namely the choice of SGD or Adam update directions for each factor and a spectral transformation of the update of B B ; the contribution lies in the principled choice of combination for each stage. Our experiments associate better SFT performance with the growth of effective rank, consistent with the joint geometry and risk trends in Section 3 . The configuration therefore departs from standard Adam in two ways. First, prior work finds that Muon promotes more uniform growth across the singular values of the LoRA increment Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} [ 15 ] . We thus apply ℳ \mathcal{M} to the update of B B to encourage spectral flattening. Second, the mechanism of effective rank in Section 3 reflects competition between coherent fitting and feedback from gradient noise. We use SGD for B B so that ℳ \mathcal{M} acts directly on the stochastic gradient’s singular directions, with the aim of encouraging the growth of the effective rank. For A A , we retain the standard Adam update, whose moment normalization can compensate for small nonzero gradients and accelerate its early evolution. Meanwhile, since B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 , unrolling the updates gives B t ​ A t = η ⁡ [ ∑ s = 0 t − 1 ℳ ⁡ ( D s B ) ] ​ A 0 + η 2 ​ [ ∑ s = 0 t − 1 ℳ ⁡ ( D s B ) ] ​ [ ∑ s = 0 t − 1 D s A ] . B_{t}A_{t}=\eta\Big[\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}\mathcal{M}(D_{s}^{B})\Big]A_{0}+\eta^{2}\Big[\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}\mathcal{M}(D_{s}^{B})\Big]\Big[\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}D_{s}^{A}\Big]. The updates to A A enter directly only through the second term, leaving the spectral flattening applied to the B B update directions in the first term unchanged.

For GRPO, our findings motivate promoting subspace rotation while preserving the within-subspace update. First, we use Adam to compute the base update directions D t A D_{t}^{A} and D t B D_{t}^{B} for the LoRA factors A A and B B , respectively, retaining adaptive scaling for both factors. Second, while applying ℳ \mathcal{M} to the full B B update distributes the update magnitude more evenly across singular directions and may also promote subspace rotation, the RL configuration further tailors the spectral transformation to target subspace rotation more directly. Define the orthogonal projector onto the current column space of B t B_{t} as P t := B t ​ ( B t ⊤ ​ B t ) † ​ B t ⊤ . P_{t}:=B_{t}(B_{t}^{\top}B_{t})^{\dagger}B_{t}^{\top}. We apply ℳ \mathcal{M} only to the component of D t B D_{t}^{B} orthogonal to this space: B t + 1 \displaystyle B_{t+1} = B t + η ⁡ [ P t ​ D t B + ℳ ⁡ ( ( I − P t ) ​ D t B ) ] , \displaystyle=B_{t}+\eta\left[P_{t}D_{t}^{B}+\mathcal{M}\!\left((I-P_{t})D_{t}^{B}\right)\right], A t + 1 \displaystyle A_{t+1} = A t + η ​ D t A . \displaystyle=A_{t}+\eta D_{t}^{A}. This update preserves the within-subspace component P t ​ D t B P_{t}D_{t}^{B} and flattens the spectrum of the orthogonal component without changing its Frobenius norm. The transformation thus specifically targets updates that move B t B_{t} beyond its current column space, providing a direct way to shape subspace rotation.

We evaluate SFT and GRPO on GSM8K and MATH. Our model suite includes Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B, and Qwen2.5-3B. Table 1 presents the GSM8K results for Llama-3.2-1B and Llama-3.2-3B, with additional results provided in Appendix A.2 . For both SFT and GRPO, we consider two baselines: standard Adam for both LoRA factors A A and B B ; and Adam base update directions D t A D_{t}^{A} and D t B D_{t}^{B} , with ℳ \mathcal{M} applied to D t B D_{t}^{B} . We additionally evaluate the dynamics-informed configurations for SFT and RL described in Section 4.1 . These comparisons examine the effects of spectral flattening, base optimizer choice, and selective treatment of the orthogonal component. Detailed experimental configurations are provided in Appendix A.2 .

As shown in Tables 1 and 2 , while applying ℳ \mathcal{M} to the full B B update with Adam directions does not consistently improve over standard Adam, the dynamics-informed configuration for SFT further replaces the Adam direction for B B with SGD and achieves the highest reported mean accuracy across all evaluated models and tasks. These comparisons highlight the benefit of combining spectral flattening with asymmetric optimization of the two LoRA factors.

The comparisons in Tables 1 , 3 , and 4 reveal a different preference for GRPO. With Adam directions for both factors, both the configuration that applies ℳ \mathcal{M} to the full B B update and the dynamics-informed RL configuration improve over standard Adam in seven of the eight model–dataset settings. Moreover, the dynamics-informed RL configuration achieves the highest reported mean accuracy in six of the eight settings. This supports the benefit of more selectively targeting the update component responsible for subspace rotation. Overall, the results favor different optimizer configurations for SFT and RL, consistent with the distinct dynamics identified in our analysis.

In this work, we identify distinct spectral and subspace dynamics of LoRA under SFT and RL. Our experiments show that RL effective rank consistently decreases during training across the learning rates considered, while for models that benefit from SFT, the growth of effective rank accompanies better SFT performance at intermediate learning rates. In addition to this difference in spectral dynamics, RL exhibits faster subspace rotation than SFT at small learning rates, with the gap narrowing as the learning rate increases. Controlled comparisons identify group-mean baseline subtraction as a key source of these differences. Using a multi-index model, our theoretical framework analyzes how baseline subtraction changes coherent fitting and feedback from gradient noise, jointly shaping effective rank, subspace rotation, and learning-rate preferences in prediction risk. These insights guide the choice of two dynamics-informed configurations for LoRA optimization, tailored to the distinct training dynamics of SFT and RL. Both configurations achieve the highest reported mean accuracy in most evaluated settings.

We further examine whether the dynamics identified in Section 2 are robust to the choice of LoRA factor initialization by reversing the default initialization: we set A 0 = 0 A_{0}=0 and use Kaiming uniform initialization for B 0 B_{0} . Figures 5 – 8 show the corresponding dynamics of effective rank and subspace overlap on GSM8K and MATH. The main qualitative observations remain consistent with those under the default initialization. For effective rank, SFT exhibits a pattern that depends on the learning rate, with effective rank decreasing at small and large learning rates while an increasing trend emerges at intermediate learning rates; in contrast, GRPO predominantly exhibits decreasing effective rank. For subspace overlap, GRPO exhibits a markedly faster decrease in overlap than SFT at small learning rates, while this gap narrows as the learning rate increases. Across both measures, SFT and RFT remain qualitatively similar, while RFT-B and GRPO form another similar pair. These results further support the conclusion from Section 2 that group-mean baseline subtraction is the primary factor underlying the observed differences in spectral and subspace dynamics. For the configuration experiments in Section 4.2 , we use fixed data partitions across all optimizer configurations. SGD uses zero momentum and zero weight decay.

Each learning rate is evaluated with three random seeds, { 7 , 42 , 44 } \{7,42,44\} . Training is run for at most 1,000 optimizer steps. We save a checkpoint and evaluate validation pass@1 every 50 optimizer steps, and stop training after three consecutive validation evaluations without a strict improvement. For each run, the checkpoint attaining the highest mean validation pass@1 is restored for final test evaluation. We then average test accuracy across the three seeds; the results in Section 4.2 report the learning rate with the highest mean accuracy over the completed sweep, together with the standard error across seeds.
